children: reported stronger quarterly results and raised its annual outlook, with shares at $585.94, up approximately 6.24%, around 11:04 a.m. ET on October 22. Third-quarter sales climbed 11% to $20.7 billion, while net earnings increased 14% to roughly $1.8 billion. The valuation picture looks less dramatic than the rally: shares sit just 2.91% above the GF Value estimate of $569.38, suggesting a modest premium to that measure.

The bigger story is the work waiting to be delivered. Backlog reached a record $292 billion, including $52.5 billion tied to a multiyear PAC-3 interceptor award. Free cash flow totaled $3 billion, although that was below the year-earlier $3.3 billion. Lockheed also lifted its annual free cash flow forecast to $7.8 billion$8 billion. Separately, Reuters reported that an initial Pentagon framework covers at least 850 U.S. F-35 aircraft over ten years, with Lockheed committing at least $7 billion to support the program.

That gives investors visibility. Turning it into cash is the harder part. The F-35 framework still requires final contract terms, pricing and schedules, while expanding production brings spending demands of its own. Lockheed warned that unresolved authorization and funding for future F-35 production could affect operations and cash flow. A record backlog strengthens the growth case, but delivery discipline and cash conversion will determine how much of that promise reaches shareholders.

title: Lockheed Martin Stocks Jump 6.24% as Backlog Hits Record
